The evidence explicitly supports all parts of the claim. 1) Regarding 'avoiding the storage of intermediate states for all parameters': The text contrasts the method with rasterization-based methods (like OpenDR and Kato et al.) that use edge rasterization passes or finite differences, implying the proposed method does not rely on storing intermediate rasterization states for all parameters but instead uses a ray-tracing based visibility engine to query the integrand directly. 2) Regarding 'explicitly handling visibility discontinuities via a boundary integral': The text repeatedly states that the derivative is decomposed into an interior term and a boundary term using Reynolds transport theorem, and the boundary term handles discontinuities (silhouettes/occlusions). 3) Regarding 'supporting transparent surfaces': The text explicitly states, 'This theory supports transparent surfaces without any modification... We do not need to resort to spatial analytical approximation'. 4) Regarding 'complex geometry without spatial analytical approximations': The text contrasts their method with Liu et al. who use sigmoid approximation (a spatial analytical approximation) and notes their method works for complex scenes without such approximations.

Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) for Differentiable Rendering provides a principled mathematical framework to compute the gradient of a rendering integral with respect to scene parameters by decomposing the derivative into an interior term (derivative of the continuous integrand) and a boundary term (integral over discontinuities) [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) provides a framework to compute the gradient of a rendering integral by decomposing it into an interior term (derivative of the continuous integrand) and a boundary term (integral over discontinuities). Source [S1] explicitly states: 'we separate its derivative integral into an interior integral and a boundary integral using Reynolds transport theorem' and defines the interior term involving the derivative of the integrand ($f'$) and the boundary term involving the difference across discontinuities ($Δf$) and boundary movement. Source [S2] similarly states that PSDR uses RTT to 'decompose the differentiation of this integral into an interior and a boundary term', where the interior term involves the derivative of the material measurement contribution function and the boundary term involves the discontinuity in the geometric term ($ΔG$). Both sources confirm the decomposition described in the claim.
